profiles.meeting_scenario: Two collaborators are planning a survey manuscript tentatively targeted at ACM Computing Surveys on design methodologies for accelerating deep learning on heterogeneous architectures. They have already collected scattered notes from a reading group and now need to turn that material into a concrete paper plan. The agenda is to finalize the survey boundary, decide the paper-collection and screening workflow, define what goes into the main comparison table, split section ownership, and set internal milestones for the next six weeks. The expected outcome is an agreed outline, a literature-gathering process, and a division of drafting responsibilities.

members.name: Dr. Leena Varma
members.role: Associate Professor leading the ML Systems group
members.expertise: Efficient deep learning, ML systems, hardware-software co-design, survey writing
members.background: Leena works on compiler/runtime support for deep learning and has previously written position papers and surveys that synthesize fast-moving systems literature for broad audiences.
members.private_state: She wants a sharply scoped, publishable survey drafted quickly so it can support an upcoming center grant proposal, and she is trying to minimize coordination overhead by keeping the review corpus curated rather than exhaustive.
hidden_assumptions: When they say "design methodology papers," they mean papers whose main contribution is a reusable workflow, tool, compiler, synthesis method, or design-space-exploration methodology, not papers whose main point is a new accelerator architecture with a small methodology subsection.

A "comparison table" in a survey should prioritize public or technically reproducible tools and should aggregate papers at the methodology-family level rather than listing every one-off framework separately.
Doing a "first pass" on the literature means a quick title-and-abstract triage in the shared spreadsheet, with full-paper extraction only after the corpus is stabilized.
The shared spreadsheet from the reading group is the practical source of truth for planning, and auxiliary citation managers are secondary.

members.name: Dr. Marco Bellini
members.expertise: DNN accelerators, architecture simulation, design space exploration, EDA toolflows
members.background: Marco comes from a hardware architecture lab and has published on accelerator evaluation frameworks, with strong familiarity with architecture venues, simulators, and toolchains used in accelerator design.
members.private_state: He wants the survey to be seen as technically authoritative by architecture reviewers and future hiring committees, and he worries that a narrow corpus will make the paper look superficial or too ML-systems-centric.
hidden_assumptions: A paper still counts as a "design methodology" contribution if it introduces a new accelerator but also contains a substantial mapping strategy, co-design loop, compiler flow, or automated exploration method.

A "comparison table" should include influential industrial and non-public toolflows if the community treats them as benchmarks or reference points, even if they are not reproducible in the open-source sense.

A "first pass" literature screen should already involve full-paper skimming, structured note-taking, and citation chasing from anchor surveys so the taxonomy is built on the complete neighborhood of each paper.
His Zotero library and coded notes are the natural source of truth because they preserve citation links, versions, and venue metadata better than a lightweight spreadsheet.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a design methodology paper
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to focus on "design methodology papers" rather than "just accelerator papers."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 interprets this as excluding papers whose primary contribution is a hardware architecture, even if they include mapping or co-design details, unless the methodology itself is the main reusable artifact.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 interprets this as including architecture papers whenever they contain a substantial exploration flow, compiler path, mapping strategy, or co-design loop that others could learn from.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely trying to avoid writing a generic accelerator catalog, so the phrase sounds aligned and disciplined; the boundary cases only appear later when curating the actual corpus.

misalignment_points.topic: What belongs in the main comparison table
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to make "one big comparison table" for the survey.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the table will cover methodology families and concrete tools that are public or described in enough detail to support a meaningful side-by-side comparison, with proprietary work mentioned only in prose.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the table should also include influential industrial compilers, internal toolflows, and one-off research frameworks if they shaped the field, even if some fields in the table are necessarily incomplete.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase "comparison table" usually signals a standard survey artifact, so neither person feels the need to restate its inclusion boundaries; both imagine the table as comprehensive in a way that feels obvious from their own community norms.

misalignment_points.topic: What the first-pass screening workflow involves
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Marco will "do the first pass" on the paper list this week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a lightweight screening pass over the existing spreadsheet: remove clearly out-of-scope items, tag papers into a few categories, and leave deep reading for the drafting phase.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a much heavier first pass: skim full papers, expand the corpus through backward and forward citation chasing, and create structured notes in Zotero before the list is considered screened.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research meetings, "first pass" naturally sounds like a shared workflow label, but labs vary widely in what effort level it implies; because both plans are reasonable, the divergence is easy to miss during a cooperative planning call.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to become a tightly scoped survey, not a sprawling accelerator census. If we anchor it around design methodology papers, we can keep the corpus curated and get a credible draft moving quickly for the center proposal. I do not want us disappearing into every architecture paper that happens to include a few pages of evaluation flow.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I think the cleanest positioning is that this should be a focused survey on design methodology papers for accelerating deep learning on heterogeneous platforms, rather than another broad catalog of accelerators. If we keep that boundary crisp, I think we can say something sharper and more useful.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, avoiding a generic architecture roundup is right, but the survey will only look authoritative if design methodology papers includes the strong architecture works where the flow, mapping, or co-design loop is really doing heavy lifting. Architecture reviewers will expect those to be represented, especially in edge and accelerator venues.
turns.utterance: I agree, that framing makes sense. We should absolutely center design methodology papers rather than just accelerator papers, while still making sure we capture the parts of the literature where the methodology is really what ties the story together.

turns.inner_thought: A structure around co-design, synthesis, compilers, and DSE will let us aggregate by reusable approach families instead of by individual hardware projects. And one big comparison table will help readers orient themselves quickly, as long as it's disciplined and doesn't devolve into an unwieldy dump of every bespoke framework.
turns.utterance: For structure, I was thinking we organize around hardware-software co-design, automated synthesis, domain-specific compilers, and design-space exploration. Then we can thread cross-cutting issues like workload assumptions and evaluation practice through those sections. And I do think we should have one big comparison table as a central artifact.

turns.inner_thought: Great, the big table should be broad enough to signal command of the field. I can pull together academic frameworks, simulator-based flows, and the industrial toolchains people constantly benchmark against or cite as de facto references, even if some entries are less complete. That will make the paper look substantial to architecture readers.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. I can take the lead on building the comparison table. I already have a decent amount of material on the academic side, and I can fold in the widely cited industrial toolchains and architecture simulators alongside the research frameworks so the table feels grounded.

turns.inner_thought: Let's keep planning anchored in the reading-group spreadsheet, since that's what everyone can see and update quickly. By first pass this week, I mean he should triage titles and abstracts, remove obvious out-of-scope items, and tag the rest. I do not want us spending days deep-reading before the corpus is stabilized.
turns.utterance: Perfect. To get moving, I suggest we start from the reading-group spreadsheet we already have, just because it gives us a common place to work from. Marco, could you do the first pass on that list this week so we can get the corpus tagged before the writing starts in earnest?

turns.inner_thought: Sure, I'll treat first pass as a real screening round: start from the spreadsheet, seed from a few anchor surveys, chase references around the key papers, skim the full texts, and code the notes properly in Zotero. The spreadsheet can be updated later, but the serious organizing should live in the citation library.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can do the first pass this week. I’ll start from the current list, seed it from a few anchor surveys, chase the citations around the key papers, and log notes in Zotero as I categorize things so we have a solid base.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If I take intro and positioning, he can cover the more architecture-adjacent technical sections. As long as those sections stay centered on design methodology papers, this division should reduce coordination overhead and let me get the framing done quickly.
turns.utterance: Great. In terms of drafting, I can take the introduction, motivation, and overall positioning section. Could you draft the sections on compilers, automated synthesis, and design-space-exploration methodologies? That seems closest to your wheelhouse.

turns.inner_thought: That works. While drafting, I'll make sure to bring in the important accelerator papers whose methodology pieces really define the taxonomy, especially for edge NPUs and heterogeneous HPC systems. Those examples are necessary if the survey is going to look technically serious beyond the ML systems audience.
turns.utterance: Yes, that fits well. As I do that, I’ll also pull in several accelerator papers whose methodology sections can help anchor the taxonomy, especially around edge NPUs and heterogeneous HPC systems.

turns.inner_thought: By next Friday I want something stable enough to write from: a reasonably cleaned spreadsheet and a comparison table with the main buckets settled. I am not expecting the universe of papers to keep expanding after that. If the scope keeps moving, the grant-support timeline is dead.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. By next Friday, I’d really like the screened corpus and the comparison table to be stable enough that I can start writing the cross-cutting challenges and open-directions sections without the ground shifting under us.

turns.inner_thought: Next Friday is tight, but I can probably have the expanded pool, coded notes, and a mostly complete table by then. The narrative can be refined afterward once we see which clusters emerge. I just hope she means stable in the sense of usable draft structure, not frozen corpus, because I expect the list to grow during citation chasing.
turns.utterance: Understood. By then I should have the expanded paper pool, the coded notes, and a nearly complete table in place so we can refine the narrative afterward rather than still debating inputs.
